📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Players have found that music in The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+’s new GTA 6-themed secret run was made with Suno, as the free DLC sits at Overwhelmingly Negative recent reviews on Steam.

Creator Edmund McMillen has since said he had no idea the music was AI-generated, with publisher Nicalis now patching it out of the game.

The run arrived in the same upgrade that brought Repentance+ to PS5, Xbox, and Switch 2 on November 19, a release date publisher Nicalis picked to go head-to-head with GTA 6.

Entering the seed V1CE BSMT unlocks a Vice City-inspired daily run with its own soundtrack, made up of seven songs plus a handful of intros and outros.

A player on the Binding of Isaac subreddit extracted the run’s music from the game files and found several tracks still carrying metadata reading “made with suno,” along with links to the songs on Suno’s site.

It has been revealed that the metadata on one track demonstrates it was created on October 30, 2026, less than three weeks before the patch went live. Other players have since checked the files and confirmed the find.

The run itself is credited to a modder known as Mr. Headcrab, who the original poster states is “staunchly anti-AI” and had no idea the music was generated.

Valve requires developers to disclose AI-generated content on a game’s Steam page, but Repentance+’s store listing makes no mention of it.

The DLC right now sits at Overwhelmingly Negative recent reviews, with only 10% of 908 reviews from the past 30 days positive, though the same update has also been blamed for breaking mods and causing crashes.

GTA 6 boss sends warning to pirates who make AI-generated PC version before official release.

GTA 6 gameplay, map, radio, and cutscene leaked ahead of Netflix Extended Look.

Modders sneak Nvidia’s leaked DLSS 5 filter into Skyrim, Control & Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth.

For some fans, the AI music is the final straw. “They used AI when synthwave is like… the easiest genre to make,” one player wrote, in a comment with dozens of upvotes.

According to recent reports, the community-run Isaac wiki has since added a note flagging the AI-generated tracks. Nicalis has yet to comment on the music or add a disclosure to the Steam page.

McMillen addressed the backlash on X, making it clear the music had been added without his knowledge.

Industry observers note that “Woke up to a sh*t show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run,” he wrote. “Looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned.”.

Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned.

Within hours, Nicalis pushed a fresh build of Repentance+, listing the “removal of generated music files” at the top of its patch notes, alongside fixes for mods broken by the launch enhancement.

Hi All!Repentance+ Upgrade:The team has pushed a new build with critical fixes.• Removal of generated music files• Larynx + Car Battery Bug Fix• PC patch—should be live already• Submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo and Sony ASAPAdditional: • Continuing work on netcode… pic.twitter.com/d1gyLUlBK8.

The patch is already live on PC, with the console versions submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo, and Sony for approval.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games has been accused of tracing a furry artist’s illustration for a decal on a custom submachine gun players can earn in GTA 6.

The gun comes from a random encounter with Chase, a fox-suited character cornered by police. Players can break through the blockade, lose the cops, and help Chase and another furry escape to the Furverts’ compound.

Chase offers the custom SMG as an alternative to cash for helping them escape. The encounter had already drawn comparisons to a real-life fursuit after players noticed shooting-star markings on Chase’s knees that resemble those on FoxiFelix’s suit.

On November 21, X user Glacius shared what they described as artwork pulled from GTA 6’s game files, including a view of the graphics used on the custom SMG. In a follow-up linking to furry artist GabyT’s work, Glacius asked, “IT WAS TRACED????”.

According to recent reports, rockstar definitely had an insider for GTA 6. Datamined furry artwork! pic.twitter.com/MjXvUz1PCq.

GabyT posted the illustration on December 8, 2021, nearly five years before GTA 6’s release. The portrait and the weapon decal both show a character with its head turned to the side, a half-lidded eye, and white fur flaring out around a dark muzzle. The version on the gun uses muddier colors and indicates the character holding a bone in its mouth.

In a recent development, commission done to Markwrc! ✅Want to see more content? Stay tuned on my social medias and watch the lives on Twitch too! ✨💻✨#wacomart #digitalart #drawing #illustration #furry #furryart #furrywolf #fantasy #animal #artwork pic.twitter.com/5dxAfFsd3X.

It has been revealed that sockz the Puppet posted a video overlaying the two images, then shared a revised comparison after lining them up on a computer. “I hope the og artist was aware and gave permission,” they wrote.

Industry observers note that bro what is this :/ I hope rockstar paid for this? https://t.co/kh35xMfHU2 pic.twitter.com/fIfvVX9vSM.

Sources indicate that the replies were split over how closely the drawings matched. X user Eli Bunny said the decal looked traced and wanted to know whether Rockstar worked with GabyT. Another user, Stick, said the images “barely line up” and described the overlap as “minor similarities.”.

Sources indicate that in a reply discussing how the artwork could have made it into the game, Sockz argued that the publisher was responsible for what it shipped. “When you publish something, it becomes your responsibility,” they wrote.

It remains unclear whether Rockstar contacted GabyT or had permission to use the illustration. Rockstar has yet to publicly address the tracing allegation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 player claims they have been banned from using PlayStation Network’s social features for 30 days after sending a friend an in-game photograph of nude NPCs.

Rockstar Games’ long-awaited GTA 6 released on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, allowing players to explore the fictional state of Leonida and its sprawling Vice City setting.

The game features a range of adult content, including nudity, which players can encounter while exploring its open world.

On November 20, X user DerrickGott007 claimed they had received a 30-day suspension from PSN’s social features after sending a friend a photograph of a nudist colony they had discovered in GTA 6.

The player stated the image was captured using the game’s built-in camera feature before being shared through PlayStation’s messaging service.

However, it appears sharing such images violates PlayStation’s Code of Conduct, which prohibits obscene or pornographic content.

Recent findings suggest that “Do not, I repeat do not send any photos taken with the in-game camera, across the PSN messaging network that contain nudity,” the post warned. “I just got a 30-day PSN social features ban for sending my friend a photo of the nudist colony in GTA 6 that I found.”.

In a recent development, DO NOT, I REPEAT DO NOT SEND ANY PHOTOS TAKEN WITH THE IN GAME CAMERA , ACROSS THE PSN MESSAGING NETWORK THAT CONTAIN NUDITY. I JUST GOT A 30 DAY PSN SOCIAL FEATURES BAN FOR SENDING MY FRIEND A PHOTO OF THE NUDIST COLONY IN GTA6 THAT I FOUND. pic.twitter.com/vsoIjmpGrt.

According to PlayStation’s official guidelines, content shared through its services can be reviewed by its safety team, with violations potentially resulting in temporary or permanent restrictions.

Sony’s policies also apply to screenshots and messages shared between players, meaning content permitted within an age-restricted game is not necessarily permitted to be distributed through PSN.

The incident serves as a warning to GTA 6 players that sharing explicit in-game photographs with friends could carry consequences beyond the game itself.

Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that weekly.
  • In a recent development, picture this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

According to recent reports, the output changes from run to run. If a user indicates "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

In a recent development, prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Sources indicate that then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

According to recent reports, the first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

Industry observers note that the second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

Sources indicate that nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

It has been revealed that A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

According to recent reports, regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email reveals up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Recent findings suggest that free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

Sources indicate that now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Industry observers note that streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Recent findings suggest that tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

Recent findings suggest that give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Sources indicate that limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

It has been revealed that A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a latest case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every fresh prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

Sources indicate that good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

After more than a decade of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 finally released on November 19, 2026, bringing players back to Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida.

Industry observers note that rockstar’s latest open-world game is packed with intricate environmental details, hidden references, and Easter eggs, with players continuing to uncover secrets scattered throughout its sprawling map. A developer who worked on the game has shared a tribute to his late mother that players can find.

In a heartfelt Instagram post, GTA 6 developer Matt Green revealed that his late mother has been honoured with a special memorial just north of the in-game region, Hamlet.

Green’s mother, Bev, passed away approximately eight months before the game’s release, meaning she never had the opportunity to see the project her son had been working on.

However, the developer was able to ensure that his mother would remain part of the game through a permanent tribute within its fictional world.

Industry observers note that “I’m incredibly grateful that she’s able to be honoured inside the world of VI – at a special memorial just north of Hamlet,” they remarked. “Miss you Mum.”.

A post shared by Matt Green (@mattxgreen).

Recent findings suggest that the developer recalled begging his mother to buy him a copy of GTA Vice City as a child. Despite her initial reluctance, she eventually agreed, a decision he believes ultimately set him on the path to working at Rockstar Games.

It has been revealed that “She was super proud and excited to see what I’d been working on but unfortunately I never got to show her,” they wrote. “She’s been gone almost 8 months now and sometimes it still doesn’t feel real.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.
  • View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays.
  • Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

Recent findings suggest that in a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube indicates it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

Industry observers note that youTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

This change is rolling out now.

According to recent reports, google has given the time picker component a Material 3 Expressive redesign, while adding a fresh scrolling variant. Meanwhile, Google AI Studio is boosting its Android app development experience.

It has been revealed that compared to Material 3, the updated M3 Expressive input and dial time pickers drop the “Select time” hint in the top-right corner, while the AM and PM buttons now benefit from expressive shape, color, and behavior. The hour and minute fields, as well as the dial selector, feature higher contrast.

The significant addition today is the scroll time picker. Instead of using the keyboard or analog clock to pick the time, you can just vertically scroll when setting an alarm or scheduling an event.

According to recent reports, nooo, the scrolling variant is what I don't like about iOS — it takes forever to dial anything in it! Why would Google copy it?

The Material Design team indicates this “compact way to select time” is “best placed inline with other content.” A keyboard icon lets you switch to the input time picker.

Use scroll time pickers instead of dial pickers when you want people to see surrounding content.

You can see various examples below:.

Google today also introduced scroll fields to select different units of measurement, like distance, weight, or temperature. In a health app, they can be used for water, calories, and more.

Clash Royale developer Supercell has recruited the creator of an advanced AI cheating tool to help crack down on cheating in the game.

AI cheating has become a growing controversy in Clash Royale, with increasingly sophisticated bots reportedly capable of outperforming skilled human players. Players highlighted claims that an AI-controlled account named ‘Clasher’ had reached the top of the game’s global leaderboard.

Sources indicate that the situation prompted calls for Supercell to intervene, with the developer addressing the controversy on November 20. In a statement posted on X, Clash Royale warned that using AI or other tools to cheat was a “royal crime,” declaring that offending players would be banished from the Arena.

On November 21, the official Clash Royale X account confirmed that it had caught the creator of an AI cheating tool and recruited them to help develop new anti-cheat technology.

It has been revealed that “The creator of the AI cheating tool has been caught,” Supercell announced in a statement framed as a royal decree from the King. “He’s agreed, entirely of his own free will, to join forces with the Clash Royale team.

“And who better to help us catch cheaters than the person who built the most advanced cheating tool we’ve seen in the Arena? Together, we’re building upcoming technology to outlaw this behaviour,” the statement concluded.

Supercell has not publicly identified the individual nor revealed if they were behind the ‘Clasher’ account. Supercell’s existing fair-play measures already combine automated detection with human moderation, including regular checks of leaderboards and competitive players.

The newly announced collaboration suggests the company is looking to strengthen those systems against increasingly sophisticated AI cheating tools.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alongside the huge list of new updates Google detailed yesterday, the firm also unveiled that a “faster and more natural” version of Gemini Live is coming to speakers and smart displays “soon.”.

Google explains this is from Gemini Live moving to the “latest speech-to-speech architecture” and brings “significantly faster response times.” Gemini Live isn’t the default experience when you start a “Hey Google” command, rather hiding behind a “let’s chat” or other similar command to start a session.

Industry observers note that initially, Live sessions were purely for brainstorming or longer conversations and lacking support for commands and other functions mid-session, but Google now indicates that this upgrade will add support for actions such as smart home controls, setting timers, and more without leaving a Live session. That’s a significant deal.

Industry observers note that coming soon – A faster and more natural Gemini Live experience: Available with a Google Home Premium subscription, Gemini Live is being upgraded to our latest speech-to-speech architecture for significantly faster response times and a smoother experience. Just say, “Hey Google, let’s chat” to brainstorm dinner ideas or plan a trip out loud, interrupt naturally to change topics, and perform actions mid-conversation—such as, setting a timer, adding a reminder,or controlling a smart home device—without stepping out of the chat³.

The “catch” is that you’ll still need a subscription to use this. Gemini Live has always required a subscription on Google Home speakers and smart displays, with the functionality looped into Google Home Premium intends which start at $10/month (or bundled into Google One AI Pro). That’s the same subscription that gives you Nest storage.

  • The driver works for Keikyu Bus, which runs services across Tokyo and Kanagawa, including routes to Haneda Airport, and the incident took place on November 16 after the bus had finished service for the day.
  • Footage of the livestream, which spread swiftly on social media, demonstrates the pair chatting on a split screen, with the streamer directing him to specific parts of the bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bus driver in Japan has been removed from driving duties after licking the hand straps and handrails inside his bus during a livestream, apparently at the request of a female streamer.

The driver works for Keikyu Bus, which runs services across Tokyo and Kanagawa, including routes to Haneda Airport, and the incident took place on November 16 after the bus had finished service for the day.

Footage of the livestream, which spread swiftly on social media, demonstrates the pair chatting on a split screen, with the streamer directing him to specific parts of the bus.

“I want you to lick the part you hold onto, a bit further up,” she remarked, according to Japanese outlet coki, to which he replied, “The part you hold?”.

【炎上】京急バス運転士、女性配信者に煽られて車内の吊り革や手すりを舐める → 会社が公式謝罪 りあきゅんとされる女性が関与したとしてSNSで物議 ↓ 女性配信者の呼びかけに応じ、男性がバス車内の吊り革や手すりを舐める様子をライブ配信 ↓ 動画がSNSで拡散され、男性が京浜急行バスの運転士だったことが判明 ↓ 11月18日、京浜急行バスが不適切行為を認めて公式謝罪。運転士を社内規則に基づき厳正に対処する方針を発表.

The streamer has been identified on social media as Riakyun, who reportedly streams on the Japanese livestreaming app Fuwatch, though Keikyu Bus did not mention her in its statement.

The driver reported himself to the organization the same day, and on November 18, Keikyu Bus posted an official apology on its website.

“We sincerely apologize for the great discomfort and concern this has caused,” the organization remarked, pledging to “thoroughly educate all employees” to prevent it from happening again.

Keikyu Bus told J-CAST News that the driver has been taken off driving duties, and that it plans to take disciplinary action against him in line with its internal rules.

The tech giant also confirmed the bus involved has been identified and fully disinfected and cleaned.

A racehorse sharing its name with IShowSpeed has claimed victory in Australia, adding another win to its growing record.

Streamer and internet personality IShowSpeed is well known for his athletic exploits, having challenged many, including fellow content creators, Olympic sprinters, and animals, to foot races.

Sources indicate that in April 2026, the streamer challenged a racehorse to a sprint during his livestreamed tour of Barbados. Despite demanding several rematches and insisting some rounds ended in draws, Speed was ultimately unable to outrun the animal.

On November 20, a horse named I Show Speed won the Jefferies Australia Class 2 Handicap at Bong Bong racecourse in Australia.

The four-year-old gelding, trained by Todd Smart and ridden by jockey Leandro Ribeiro, finished 1.3 lengths ahead of second-place Mystic Air in the 1,000-metre race.

According to Racenet’s racing records, this marked the horse’s third career victory, having previously won races at Canberra Acton in July 2025 and June 2026.

A post shared by SKY Racing (@skyracingau).

The horse actually has a heartwarming backstory. According to a statement from Todd Smart Racing, I Show Speed was born prematurely, but overcame its difficult start to win its debut race in July 2025.

“We couldn’t be prouder of our little fighter I SHOW SPEED,” the stable wrote, when celebrating its debut victory.

Despite the racehorse sharing its name with the streamer, it remains unclear whether the horse was deliberately named after the streamer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many services are turning to AI in place of an actual human being, Pebblebee’s latest Alert Dispatch brings the help of a real person into an emergency situation, and it all starts with your Find Hub tracker.

Pebblebee launched its Alert feature in 2025 as a way to use a Clip 5 tracker for Find Hub as a siren in an emergency. The company later added an optional live location-sharing feature to this, and also released “Halo” as an emergency siren first, tracker second with a special design.

Now, “Alert Dispatch” takes the whole system up a notch.

It has been revealed that instead of relying solely on location sharing and the siren, Pebblebee’s Alert Dispatch assigns an actual human being to the situation, with a trained dispatch agent reaching out first over SMS or a call, then pulling in emergency responders if the situation calls for it. The feature works with Clip 4, Clip 5, and Halo.

Sources indicate that alert Dispatch connects Pebblebee users with a trained dispatch agent when they trigger an Alert, starting with a text and escalating to an Emergency call if they don’t respond. With an attempt to send help when users cannot confirm they’re safe, plus live location sharing and private Check-In calls on Clip 5 and Halo, it adds another layer of support when calling for help isn’t an option.

Industry observers note that pebblebee Alert Dispatch runs in partnership with Noonlight, with an alert triggered by disconnecting Halo or rapidly pressing the button on Clip trackers. Pricing is as follows:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a newly introduced Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

Industry observers note that meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

Meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the company’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

So this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

A family-owned restaurant called Oscar’s has been left stunned after discovering that their business seemingly appears in GTA 6.

GTA 6 has finally arrived, allowing players to explore Rockstar Games’ fictional state of Leonida, which takes heavy inspiration from Florida and features countless locations modelled on real-life landmarks.

Since its November 19 release, players have been discovering familiar locations throughout the game, but one family was particularly surprised to find their own restaurant recreated in Rockstar’s open world.

On November 21, X user @sirenaslloran shared her emotional reaction after discovering that her family’s restaurant, Oscar’s, had seemingly been recreated in GTA 6.

Industry observers note that “Guys my family’s restaurant made it onto GTA 6. I’m crying so bad,” she wrote. “My parents are immigrants who came here with a dream and now we’ve been voted by the city as the number one breakfast spot and now this.”.

She explained that her parents had immigrated to the United States hoping to build a successful business and that their restaurant had since been voted the city’s number-one breakfast spot.

Oscar’s has two locations and is family owned & operated ! Thank you so much for the support & kind messages. I’m reading them all to my family & my abuela says “gracias y que Dios los bendiga siempre”. 🩷 https://t.co/9EgmdobDsj pic.twitter.com/8fIGviTcnU.

In a follow-up post, she revealed that Oscar’s is a family-owned and operated business with two locations. She also explained that she had been reading the messages aloud to her family, sharing a particularly touching response from her grandmother.

“Gracias y que Dios los bendiga siempre,” her grandmother mentioned, which translates to “Thank you, and may God always bless you.”.

Recent findings suggest that A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report indicates two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

In a recent development, this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

In a recent development, before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a latest purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

According to recent reports, this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

In a recent development, keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

Recent findings suggest that the browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

In a recent development, forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

Recent findings suggest that there are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Sources indicate that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

According to recent reports, store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

According to recent reports, caller ID is a separate problem. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

"data": { "status": "completed" }.

It has been revealed that the event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

In a recent development, resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, problem a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

In a recent development, authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

It has been revealed that A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id).

Industry observers note that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a fresh event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

Sources indicate that the function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

According to recent reports, after this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

In a recent development, for voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Industry observers note that imagine the CRM saves an upgrade, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

Industry observers note that if the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

It has been revealed that also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events enhancement the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

In a recent development, have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

According to recent reports, then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

It has been revealed that operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Recent findings suggest that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Recent findings suggest that start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

Industry observers note that it is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

It has been revealed that sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

Industry observers note that you can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Sources indicate that keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

VAST indicates petabyte SSDs will outgrow today’s parallel file system RAID

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, VAST Data says petabyte SSDs will outgrow RAID in today’s parallel file systems, according to a simulation of its own 900 PB system that puts the odds of data loss at 1 in 11 over 10 years.
  • Bigger drives take longer to rebuild after a failure, leaving more time for further failures to lose data, but operators will still want those large drives because many sites are power-constrained and storage power scales with bandwidth rather than capacity.
  • The manufacturer’s principal technical strategist, Glenn Lockwood, walked through the simulation, described as a “discrete event simulation” using real failure data, in an Exhibitor Forum talk during SC26’s HPC System Hardware and Architecture session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, VAST Data says petabyte SSDs will outgrow RAID in today’s parallel file systems, according to a simulation of its own 900 PB system that puts the odds of data loss at 1 in 11 over 10 years. At Supercomputing 2026 (SC26), the company explains how.

Bigger drives take longer to rebuild after a failure, leaving more time for further failures to lose data, but operators will still want those large drives because many sites are power-constrained and storage power scales with bandwidth rather than capacity. VAST’s recommended fix: system-wide erasure coding with at least three parity strips.

The manufacturer’s principal technical strategist, Glenn Lockwood, walked through the simulation, described as a “discrete event simulation” using real failure data, in an Exhibitor Forum talk during SC26’s HPC System Hardware and Architecture session. With petabyte-scale SSDs swapped in, enclosure-local declustered RAID — the approach used by DDN EXAScaler and HPE Cray ClusterStor, per Lockwood — has those exceptionally high odds of data loss. With global declustering and extra parity, operators can get this down to 1 in 54 million, a significant improvement, but VAST’s own scheme gets to about 1 in 62 billion, three orders of magnitude better.

It has been revealed that lockwood’s case for petabyte SSDs rests on how storage power scales: at about 28 W per SSD, regardless of capacity and including its share of the surrounding infrastructure, plus 20 W per GB/s of bandwidth. Getting 900 PB of flash from 15 TB SSDs would take more than 63K drives, each adding its own bandwidth, for 190 TB/s at 5.6 MW, or “the equivalent of 3,100 or so of Blackwell Ultra GPUs.” Lockwood states, though, that “real AI applications in our experience have never approached needing anything close to that level of performance” from the storage.

Sources indicate that with 122 TB drives, at almost an 8K count and much lower 8 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth, the power draw is less than a tenth of that, at about 400 kW. Within that budget, 15 TB SSDs top out at about 250 PB, even with no power left for performance. That power could be better spent on compute and, anyway, 245 TB-class drives are already arriving, with much larger drives expected.

Everything is a series of trade-offs, though, and larger drives come with their own caveats. Lockwood acknowledges the usual reaction to a 245 TB drive: that it’s “a substantial blast radius,” since a single failure leaves much more to rebuild. And it does take longer: at the same per-drive speed, a 122 TB drive takes twice as long to rebuild as a 60 TB drive, leaving a longer window in which a second failure in a traditional RAID 5 set loses data. Per-drive capacity is potentially outpacing bandwidth increases and, at least within a generation, “the performance of each individual drive does not change,” so this is something that must be accepted or overcome.

The simulated system involves 7,920 SSDs at 122 TB each, using 180 enclosures with 44 drives each. With a RAID 5 single parity solution, there is a 100% chance of data loss over 10 years, but “no one uses single parity anymore.” Double parity still has 1 in 150 odds of data loss over a decade and is considered “state of the art for many open source file systems,” and he explicitly names Lustre and BeeGFS within this context.

For proprietary parallel file system implementations, declustered RAID within an enclosure is the state of the art, instead. Declustered RAID spreads each drive group’s data, parity, and spare space over more drives than usual, allowing for faster rebuilds. Keeping it within an enclosure means that the spread still stays within a single box of drives. Swapping petabyte SSDs into that enclosure-level declustering is what gets to the headline 1 in 11 odds of data loss.

As for the mentioned rivals, DDN’s DCR, in one published configuration, uses RAID 6 in an 8+2 array for a 24-NVMe SSD pool. That means eight data strips plus two parity strips per stripe, allowing any two drives in the pool to fail without losing data, and each stripe is spread over 10 of the 24 drives. DDN has conceded in the past that larger systems may need more than DCR. HPE’s declustered RAID solution is known as GridRAID, with declustered parity per enclosure half, meaning two 12-drive pools per 24-drive enclosure.

According to recent reports, perlmutter, the supercomputer at Berkeley Lab’s National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, where Lockwood once worked, used GridRAID with 8+2+1 RAID 6 per 12-drive object storage target, Lustre’s name for a storage unit. The +1 is one spare drive’s worth of space, spread across all 12, so a rebuild writes to every surviving drive rather than to a single replacement. Either way, protection stops at two failures in a pool of one or two dozen drives, and only those drives can assist with a rebuild. This is the scenario in VAST’s simulation with the catastrophic failure rate.

Odds of data loss over 10 years.

Open-source Lustre and BeeGFS, typically.

Declustered RAID within an enclosure.

DDN EXAScaler, HPE Cray ClusterStor.

Declustered RAID across the whole system, plus extra parity.

VAST’s own scheme (not detailed).

Industry observers note that several solutions exist, with limits. Adding a parity strip for triple parity reduces the odds of data loss. Global declustering, on its own, can also reduce the odds a little bit, with faster rebuild times. However, stripes are spread over every drive in the cluster, so two random failures are more likely to hit the same stripe, meaning a larger fault domain.

If both approaches are used, which is the minimum bar for him, you get down to getting struck by “lightning on your birthday” odds. VAST already publishes quadruple parity, which is beyond this bar. Using VAST’s own “special magic,” undisclosed but beyond the minimum bar, drops the odds even further, specifically for the petabyte SSDs, which is the real target of the talk.

Recent findings suggest that then we get to the metadata, the data about data, which in this case is the index of where every piece of every file dwells. Every write necessarily updates it synchronously, so VAST keeps it on separate, fast SSDs as three full copies for replication, not parity. This means it can survive two failures, which is less than the data’s four parity strips, and the index becomes the weakest link. With 122 TB drives, he puts the data drives’ odds at 1 in 78 trillion over 10 years, against 1 in 58 million for metadata. To Lockwood, this illustrates that the surrounding infrastructure is the real risk, given the failure gap between the index and regular data.

Industry observers note that rebuilding in the index area starts about 12 seconds after a failure, on average, versus about two minutes for data drives, Lockwood says. VAST’s procedure more generally, for when a drive drops out, is to power-cycle it and hope, so there is always some delay before a rebuild is forced. This slight delay barely matters for data drives with four parity strips but is more impactful for the three-copy metadata index drives. For example, waiting an hour for data drives “wouldn’t make a big difference” while just 20 minutes or more on a metadata drive has “extremely high” risk.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, in May, Micron began shipping the 245 TB 6600 ION, which pulls up to 30 W at maximum load. Kioxia has the LC9, used in a Dell 2U server with 40 drives for a total of 9.8 PB. SanDisk also has its 256 TB UltraQLC, which was due in the first half of this year, and Solidigm is targeting about 245 TB later this year.

Meanwhile, multiple roadmaps reach petabyte-class drives, including SanDisk’s UltraQLC, a target by SK hynix for QLC SSDs, and Samsung at some time in the future. This strengthens VAST’s case and, while at least the power math adds up, data still needs to be compared openly and fairly to make a firm conclusion about the best pathway forward for what is clearly an unavoidable problem.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

Google Wallet is preparing another form of digital ID storage, with support for your Social Security card apparently on the way.

According to recent reports, you can already store your passport or select State driver’s licenses in Google Wallet in the US, and it seems Google isn’t stopping there. Wallet now appears to be preparing some level of support for storing a digital copy of your Social Security card, as code in the latest app updates suggest.

According to recent reports, there’s zero reason to store your SS card like this. Unnecessary exposure.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted explicit references to “Social Security Number” in Google Play Services v26.46.30 in connection with Google Wallet.

While exact functionality is unclear at this time, this appears to include support for seeing your Social Security benefits, or at least logging those benefits, in a digital form. There are mentions of Retirement, Survivors, and/or Disability Insurance (RSDI), Supplemental Security Income, Medicare, and more, as well as qualifiers for deductions and effective dates.

#138503. Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1800 w)

Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.
  • Recent findings suggest that many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout.
  • According to recent reports, the below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

Recent findings suggest that many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it….

According to recent reports, the below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

The number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

It has been revealed that in the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!).

Rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However….

While it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

In a recent development, A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

According to recent reports, there are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

In a recent development, rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

Recent findings suggest that car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're quickly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to quickly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

Sources indicate that this might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying latest garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Recent findings suggest that throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions new options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.
